011.subtitle: The lute silenced, and a mind gone under

commentary.meaning: Still the mouth, but no longer its parts — now what comes out of it. The first name sets her speech against the kacchapī, the lute that belongs to the goddess of speech herself, and the lute loses; and the word chosen for what she says is not song, not mantra, not oratory, but sallāpa, ordinary friendly talk. Her chat outsings the best instrument there is. The second name goes back to the smile the hymn has been circling since the tenth verse and finds a new thing for it to do: light comes off it in such quantity that the mind of her husband sinks and does not come up. Both names describe an effect on somebody else rather than a feature of her, which is a change of method. The description pauses to record two casualties — an instrument shamed into silence, and a mind under water — and the second casualty is the first appearance in this hymn of the god she is married to.
commentary.history:
Kacchapī is a female tortoise. Monier-Williams gives that sense first and then adds the second: a kind of lute, so named because it is shaped like a tortoise, and he cross-refers to the Latin testudo — the shell-bodied instrument of the classical Mediterranean, the Greek chelys, which was made from a real tortoise. The dictionary is pointing at a coincidence between two unrelated musical traditions, and it happens to be exactly right about why the Sanskrit word exists: the resonator is a curved bowl. In the Indian tradition Kacchapī is the proper name of Sarasvatī's instrument, as Mahatī is the name of Nārada's. So the first name of this verse is not comparing her speech to a lute in general. It is naming a specific instrument belonging to a specific goddess and saying that this goddess's small talk defeats it.

Śaṅkara stages the whole scene, and reading his verse beside the name is the quickest way to see what the sixteen syllables are compressing. Sarasvatī is singing Śiva's exploits to her lute. Devī begins to say something appreciative and moves her head as she says it. That is all: one word of praise, offered in passing. And the sweetness of it so contradicts the delicate ringing of the strings that Vāṇī, without a word, slips the cloth cover back over her vīṇā and puts it away. Nothing is announced and nobody is humiliated in public. The Vāgdevatās fold that into a single participle.

That participle is worth pressing on. Vinirbhartsita is built on the causative of a root that means to threaten, to scold, to revile — Monier-Williams glosses the related noun bhartsana as threatening, menace, curse — and it is armed with two prefixes, vi and nis, which push it to an extreme. So the lute has not merely been surpassed. It has been shouted down. The two names of the ninth verse defeated coral and the bimba fruit, but those were fruit and stone; this is the first time the losing party in one of these contests is a person, and the verb has become correspondingly harsh. There is a small joke in that harshness, since what does the shouting down is the gentlest sound in the poem.

The second half returns to a construction the hymn used twenty-two names ago and repeats it almost exactly. The sixth name was nijāruṇaprabhāpūramajjadbrahmāṇḍamaṇḍalā: her own light, prabhā, in flood, pūra, with the world-eggs majjat, drowning in it. Here it is mandasmitaprabhāpūramajjatkāmeśamānasā: the light of her faint smile, in flood, with Kāmeśa's mind drowning in it. Same noun, same noun, same present participle, in the same order and the same metrical position. This is self-quotation across a distance, and the substitution at the end is the whole point. What went under the first time was the entire ring of world-eggs. What goes under this time is one mind. The scale shrinks and the claim grows, because of whose mind it is.

Kāmeśa, lord of desire, is Śiva under the name this tradition prefers for him, and nāma 28 is the first place in the whole text — meditation verses included — where the consort is named at all. He arrives already submerged. That is not accidental placement. The first verse of the Saundaryalaharī states the doctrine flatly: joined with Śakti, Śiva can act; without her he cannot stir. The stotra makes the same point without arguing it, by choosing the moment of his first appearance to describe him as unconscious in her light.

One small thing the vocabulary allows, which may or may not have been meant. Mānasa is an ordinary word for the mind, and Monier-Williams also records it as the name of the lake Mānasa in the Himālaya, the water the wild geese are supposed to fly to. Kāmeśamānasa can be heard, without any violence to the grammar, as Kāmeśa's lake — which is a convenient thing to be drowning in. The hymn does not say this. The language makes it available.
commentary.practice:
Two sixteen-syllable names, one to a line, and for once both caesurae fall in a helpful place. Count eight in the first line and you land exactly at the end of mādhurya: nijasallāpamādhurya, then vinirbhartsitakacchapī. Count eight in the second and you land at the end of pūra: mandasmitaprabhāpūra, then majjatkāmeśamānasā. In both cases the break in the metre is also a break in the compound, so the natural breath and the natural sense agree. That is not always true in this hymn and it is worth enjoying when it happens.

Sallāpa hides a rule. The underlying form is saṃlāpa, from sam plus √lap, to talk; the nasal has assimilated forward into the l and doubled it. Monier-Williams is severe about it and files sallāpa as a wrong reading for saṃlāpa, but the doubled form is thoroughly current and it is what the stotra has. Say sal-lā-pa with the l held long enough to be counted twice, because the metre counts the first syllable heavy on the strength of it.

Vinirbhartsita is the hardest word in the verse and probably in the last five. Break it vi-nir-bhart-si-ta. The r of nir survives before a voiced consonant instead of becoming a visarga, so you get r running directly into the aspirated bh: let the breath be heard. Then bhart-si gives you r, an unaspirated dental t and a dental s in immediate succession, which is a sequence English never asks for. Slow it to three separate gestures and then close the gap. Note in passing that the nāmāvalī printed with this recension writes the dative as vinirbhatsitakacchapyai, without the r; the stotra line has it, and it belongs there.

Kacchapī gives you the cch you met at radanacchadā in the ninth verse, but this time it is inside the stem rather than at a junction between words. Give the first c a clean closure before the aspirated ch, and keep both of them as affricates made at the hard palate, never as the k sound English would supply.

The second line is easier but has two places to lose. Majjat is the doubled palatal you have now met three times — ujjvalā at the end of verse two, majjat in verse three, ujjvalā again at the end of verse ten — and it must be heard as two j sounds. Immediately after it comes a t running into a k in majjatkāmeśa: both unvoiced, both stops, and the temptation is to swallow the t. Release it.

Vowel lengths carry the sense here. Nija is two short syllables and means one's own, innate; if you lengthen it, it becomes nothing. Mādhurya and kacchapī both end long. In the second line, manda, smita and majjat are all short and quick, and then prabhā, pūra, kāmeśa and mānasā open out into long vowels one after another — which is a fair imitation of a flood.

For the recitation as archanā, the two names take the dative in -yai: nijasallāpamādhuryavinirbhartsitakacchapyai namaḥ, mandasmitaprabhāpūramajjatkāmeśamānasāyai namaḥ. Notice that the ī-stem contracts to -yai while the ā-stem keeps a syllable and gives -āyai. Saying the two one after the other is the cleanest short lesson in feminine datives the hymn offers.

As for what to hold: this is the verse in which the poem stops looking and starts listening. The instruction it implies is unusually concrete. Attend to the fact that what defeated the best music available was not a performance but a passing remark, and that what put the god of desire out of his mind was not a display but a slight smile. Nothing in this verse is done on purpose.

012.subtitle: The chin no one has matched, and a knotted thread

commentary.meaning: The description resumes its downward march and takes one step at a time. First the chin — and the name does something new. Since the ninth verse the method has been to produce a standard of comparison and then defeat it: a ruby mirror, coral, the bimba fruit. Here no standard is produced. Anākalita means not grasped, never arrived at; the poets went looking for something to set beside her chin and came back empty-handed, and the name says that she shines by their failure. Then the neck, and on it the only ornament in this entire head-to-foot description that is not a jewel or a flower. It is a thread. Kāmeśa tied it there. A verse that has just admitted that language cannot reach a chin turns out to be perfectly able to describe a piece of string, and the string outranks everything else that has been put on her so far.
commentary.history:
Start with the spelling of the chin, because it is a small lesson in how this vocabulary behaves. Monier-Williams's headword is cubuka, and he records cibuka and chubuka as the same word. The stotra uses cibuka; Śaṅkara, in the verse that covers the same feature, uses cubuka. Neither is a mistake. The word simply wobbles in its first vowel across the tradition, as a handful of body-part words do, and a reader who looks for cibuka in the dictionary will be sent to cubuka. Worth knowing before it happens.

What Śaṅkara does with the chin is instructive precisely because he ends where the sahasranāma begins. His last word is aupamyarahitam, devoid of comparison — the same verdict as anākalitasādṛśya. But he spends the three lines before it describing the chin anyway, and he does it entirely through what has been done to it rather than what it looks like. Her father the snow mountain touches it with his fingertips out of fondness. Her husband tips it up, again and again, impatient to drink from her lip. And it is the handle of a mirror: Sanskrit hand-mirrors were polished metal discs with a stem to hold them by, so calling her chin the stem of a mirror makes her face the disc and makes Śiva the one looking into it. Three actions and one metaphor, and then the confession that none of it amounts to a comparison. The stotra keeps only the confession.

The second name is one of the clearest regional fingerprints in the whole hymn. A māṅgalyasūtra is the auspicious cord tied round the bride's neck by the groom — the tāli of Tamil and Malayalam usage, the maṅgalasūtra of Marathi and Kannada. It is not a Vedic rite. The classical wedding ceremony described in the gṛhya literature has the taking of the hand, the seven steps and the mounting of the stone, and no thread of this kind; the tying of the tāli is a later and largely southern and western custom that the stotra treats as simply what happens at a wedding. Together with the Gopura-crowned city that this hymn will describe at name fifty-six, and the temple-shaped ornaments and southern flowers scattered through it, this name is part of the evidence that places the text's composition in the south.

It also settles a debt the hymn incurred six verses ago. Name twenty-five called her face the wedding house of Love and made her eyebrows the toraṇa flung over its doorway, using the word māṅgalya for the occasion. Five names later the same word returns, and now the wedding announced over the door has been performed and there is a knot at the throat to prove it. The hymn is not repeating an image; it is finishing a sentence.

Śaṅkara's verse on the throat makes the connection explicit in a way the compressed name cannot. He looks at the three fine lines that run across her neck and calls them pratibhū — a legal word, meaning a surety, one who stands guarantor for another's obligation — for the number of well-twisted strands bound on at her wedding. Three lines, three strands, and the throat itself keeps the record. Then, in the same breath, he reads the three lines a second time as the boundary markers that fix the standing of the three grāmas, the three basic scale-systems of classical Indian music. The one throat is at once a marriage register and a musical instrument, which is exactly the pair of things the previous verse of this hymn was talking about.

A final caution about a word. Kandharā, the neck, is not a headword in Monier-Williams under that spelling; he has kaṃdhara, and he derives it from kam, the head, plus dhara from √dhṛ, to hold — so it means the head-holder. That etymology is worth carrying while you chant the name, because the thing this head-holder is described as holding is not the head but a thread that somebody else put there. The dictionary also records kaṃdhara as a word for a cloud, on the other sense of kam, water; nothing in the verse needs that, but it is the kind of thing that turns up when you look.

There is one theological point that the tradition never fails to draw. Every ornament described in the last nine verses has been shown to derive its value from her: the flowers borrow her fragrance, the stars turn themselves into rubies to be in her crown, the coral and the bimba lose. The thread is the exception. It came from outside her, it was tied by someone else, and it is the one item the hymn names its donor for. That the marriage cord of a goddess whose husband cannot die is a permanent object is the plain sense the tradition takes from the name.
commentary.practice:
Two sixteen-syllable names, one per line, with clean caesurae again: anākalitasādṛśya, then cibukaśrīvirājitā; kāmeśabaddhamāṅgalya, then sūtraśobhitakandharā.

The first word teaches a rule that will save you elsewhere. The negative prefix is a- before a consonant and an- before a vowel, so a-kalita but an-ākalita — precisely as Greek has a-theos and an-arkhos. Say a-nā-ka-li-ta and hear the n as the joint, not as part of the stem. The stem is ākalita, from ā plus √kal, to reckon or make out; anākalita is what has not been reckoned.

Sādṛśya contains the syllabic ṛ inside a conjunct, dṛ, and then the cluster śya. Take it as sā-dṛ-śya, with the ṛ short — one beat, tongue in the retroflex position — and with the ś of śya made at the hard palate along with the y that follows it. That is the third syllabic ṛ you have met, after mṛganābhi in verse five and gṛha in verse six.

The second line opens with a piece of Sanskrit spelling worth stopping for. Baddha is written बद्ध: an unaspirated d followed by an aspirated dh. Sanskrit does not double an aspirate. When a rule calls for a doubled aspirated consonant, the first copy loses its breath, so bh becomes b-bh, dh becomes d-dh, kh becomes k-kh. You will meet this everywhere once you can see it. Say bad-dha, closing the first d fully before releasing the aspiration on the second.

Māṅgalya gives you ṅg, the guttural nasal made at the same place as the g that follows, and then the cluster ly — you met both in māṅgalya at verse six, so this is the second run at the same word. Sūtra needs a long ū and then the cluster tr with a dental t. Śobhita has the palatal ś at the head and an aspirated bh in the middle; keep the aspiration.

The sibilants in this verse are a good short drill because they are all one kind. Sādṛśya, śrī, śobhita: the first s in sādṛśya is dental, the ś in the same word is palatal, and śrī and śobhita are palatal. There is no retroflex ṣ anywhere in the verse. Chanting it slowly with attention to that one contrast, dental s against palatal ś, is worth doing twice.

One sandhi is invisible in both scripts and must be reconstructed. Cibuka plus śrī gives cibukaśrī with nothing hidden, but virājitā at the end of the first name and anvitā-type endings elsewhere in the hymn are all past participles doing the same job: made resplendent by. Virājita is vi plus √rāj, to shine, in the past participle, and the vi- intensifies. Hearing it as a participle rather than as part of the noun makes the whole sixteen syllables resolve into a subject and a predicate.

For the archanā, the datives are anākalitasādṛśyacibukaśrīvirājitāyai namaḥ and kāmeśabaddhamāṅgalyasūtraśobhitakandharāyai namaḥ — both plain ā-stems, both taking -āyai, and the second of them is one of the longest single words you will be asked to say in the fourth case anywhere in the hymn.

On what to hold: the two names are a matched pair about the limits of description. The first says that a chin defeated every poet who tried it. The second says that the most important thing on her body is a piece of thread, and describes it exactly. The counsel implied is not to assume that the grand things are the ones that matter.

013.subtitle: Gold on the arms, pearls at the throat

commentary.meaning: Two names that end in the same word, anvitā, endowed with — and Sanskrit does not rhyme, so when a poet makes two lines close on the identical sound he is telling you to take them together. The arms first, with two named ornaments: the aṅgada and the keyūra, both worn on the upper arm, distinguished by jewellers and not distinguishable in English. Then the throat again, one layer out from the thread that was tied there in the previous verse: a jewelled collar, the pendant hung from it, and strings of loose pearls swinging below. What is striking is how little either name claims. Nothing is outshone, nothing is put to shame, nothing is said to be beyond comparison. After eight verses of contests, the hymn simply lists what she is wearing, and the effect of a list is the effect a list always has. It is an inventory of wealth.
commentary.history:
Aṅgada and keyūra are both glossed by Monier-Williams as a bracelet worn on the upper arm, in almost the same words, and putting the two together in one compound is the ordinary Sanskrit way of saying that she is wearing a full set — as English might say rings and bracelets without meaning to draw a line between them. Where the two are distinguished in practice, keyūra is generally the band worn high, above the elbow, and aṅgada the one on the arm below it, but usage varies between texts and between regions, and it would be an overstatement to say the compound is being precise. What is precise is the metal. Kanaka is gold, and this is the first metal named anywhere in the description. Everything up to now has been stone, flower, light or thread.

The arms have been counted once already. The sixth name of the hymn was cāturbāhusamanvitā, endowed with four arms, and it used the same participle in a slightly longer form. That was arithmetic; this is dressing. Between the two lies everything the hands were shown holding — the noose, the goad, the sugarcane bow, the five arrows — so by the time the hymn puts gold on those arms the reader knows what they are for.

Śaṅkara gives the four arms a verse of their own and finds an unexpected reason to care about the number. Brahmā, who is lotus-born and has four faces, praises her four arms with all four mouths at once — and the reason he is so anxious to do it is that Śiva once tore off his fifth head with a fingernail. Terrified of those nails ever since, he wants a gesture of protection extended to each remaining head simultaneously, and he thinks flattery of exactly the right number of arms may procure it. It is a joke, and it is also a demonstration of how completely the tradition assumes that the count of her limbs is a live theological quantity rather than an artistic convention.

Graiveya, the word for the necklace, is built on grīvā, the throat. Monier-Williams gives it as a necklace and then, in the neuter and masculine, as a chain worn round the neck of an elephant. The overlap is not a pun the verse is making, but it is a fair reminder that this vocabulary is not sentimental about the difference between adorning a woman and harnessing an animal, and that both meanings are about weight hung from a neck. Elephants will be along in due course, at name sixty-six.

Cintāka, the pendant, is a genuine gap. It is not a headword in Monier-Williams at all. The sense given here — a drop or ornament hung from the middle of a necklace — is what the context requires and what the commentators supply, and it is the sense the word carries in the ornament lists of this kind of literature; but a student working from the dictionary alone will find nothing, exactly as with cillikā in the sixth verse. Note in passing that the same first element turns up later in the hymn in a much more famous compound, cintāmaṇigṛha, the house built of the wish-granting stone, at name fifty-seven. Whether the pendant is being named for the stone or the stone for the shape of a pendant is not something the text answers.

Lola, the word for the way the pearls hang, is one of the more interesting adjectives in this stotra. Monier-Williams gives moving hither and thither, shaking, rolling, tossing, dangling, swinging, agitated, unsteady, restless — and then, in a second block of senses, changeable, transient, fickle, and then desirous, greedy. It is the standard epithet of a beautiful woman's eyes and the standard epithet of Lakṣmī, who never stays. Applied to pearls on a string it means nothing more than swinging, but the word arrives carrying its other lives.

Muktā, the pearl, is the best single word in the verse. Monier-Williams defines it as a pearl, and then explains the derivation in a parenthesis: as loosened from the pearl-oyster shell. It is the past participle of √muc, to release — the same root that gives mukti, liberation. A pearl in Sanskrit is a released thing, and a hymn that will end with a promise of release has hung a string of them at her throat.

Śaṅkara's verse on the necklace supplies the mythology behind the pearls and one of his best conceits. The pearls, he says, began from the frontal bosses of the elephant demon — an allusion to the belief, set out in the gemmological chapters of Varāhamihira's Bṛhat Saṃhitā, that pearls are found not only in oysters but in elephants, conches, clouds, bamboo, snakes, fish and boars, with the elephant pearl the rarest and finest. Those white pearls then take on a mottling from within, because the red of her lips is reflected in them, and so the whole necklace comes to look like the fame of the destroyer of the three cities, shot through with the red of his valour. Fame in Sanskrit poetry is white and valour is red, and the necklace has become a diagram of her husband's reputation.
commentary.practice:
Both names run to sixteen syllables and both end in -ānvitā, so the verse is audibly a couplet. Anvita is anu plus the past participle of √i, to go: gone along with, accompanied by, endowed with. Say an-vi-tā and let the nv be two distinct consonants; English tends to nasalize through it.

The first line opens on a sandhi you cannot hear and can barely see. Kanaka plus aṅgada gives kanakāṅgada: a short a and a short a have merged into one long ā, written with a single ा, and the seam is gone. This is the same merger as campakāśoka in the fourth verse and nijāruṇa in the third. It is the commonest sandhi in the hymn and the commonest cause of mis-parsing a long name.

Keyūra needs a long e. Sanskrit has no short e; the vowels e and o are always long, being contractions of a plus i and a plus u. Learners who come to the language through modern Indian pronunciations tend to clip it, and the metre will not allow that. Ke-yū-ra, with the ū long as well.

Kamanīya rewards a moment. It is a gerundive from √kam, to desire — the same root as kāma — so what it says is not lovely but to-be-desired. The suffix -anīya is one of the two ways Sanskrit forms a gerundive, and once you can hear it you will find it all over the literature. The arms are not described as beautiful; they are described as things that ought to be wanted.

In the second line, ratna gives you tn, a dental stop running into a dental nasal with no movement of the tongue at all — one of the easiest clusters in the language and one of the most often fumbled, because English has no word with that sequence inside a syllable. Graiveya opens with gr and then the diphthong ai, which is long: grai-ve-ya. Muktāphala has the kt cluster and then ph, which is an aspirated p and never the English f; let the p close and the breath follow, as in sphurat in the meditation verses.

Both caesurae fall cleanly at the eighth syllable and both fall inside a compound rather than between its members: kanakāṅgadakeyūra breaks after keyūra, which is a joint, but ratnagraiveyacintāka breaks after cintāka, which is also a joint. The verse is unusually well behaved.

There is one nāmāvalī slip worth knowing about, because it is the sort of thing that makes a learner doubt his own reading. The dative form printed with this recension for the thirty-first name reads kanakāṅgadakeyūrakamanīyamujānvitāyai, with muja for bhuja. The stotra line has bhuja, arm, which is the only form that makes sense. Copyists drop aspirates.

For the archanā the two names are kanakāṅgadakeyūrakamanīyabhujānvitāyai namaḥ and ratnagraiveyacintākalolamuktāphalānvitāyai namaḥ. Said one after the other they are almost the same length and end identically, which is the point at which the rhyme in the stotra becomes impossible to miss.

On what to hold: there is no argument in this verse and no comparison to work out, and the temptation is therefore to hurry it. Resist that. What the hymn is doing here is the oldest thing a devotional description does — counting the wealth of the person being described, item by item, because counting is a form of attention. Take the gold, then the pendant, then the pearls, and let the pearls swing.

014.subtitle: A stake laid down, and a creeper in the garden

commentary.meaning: Both names describe the same part of the body and arrive at it by routes that have nothing in common. The first is commercial. Her husband's love is a jewel; her breasts are the pratipaṇa, the counter-stake — the thing the second player puts on the table to match what the first has already put there. Two objects of equal worth are set against one another and neither party is out of pocket. The second name is horticultural, and it reads her whole midriff as a piece of gardening: the navel is the ālavāla, the shallow basin a gardener scrapes out round the root of a young tree so that water will soak in where it is wanted; the line of down above it is the creeper growing out of that basin; her two breasts are the fruit the creeper has borne. So the verse looks twice at one thing and produces first a market and then a garden — a transaction between equals, and something that grew.
commentary.history:
Pratipaṇa comes from gambling. Monier-Williams gives it as the stake of an adversary at play, and then, on the other derivation, as barter or exchange; the underlying paṇa is a bet, the sum played for, and also a copper weight used as coin. So the name has been built out of the vocabulary of the gaming board and the market stall, which is not where a hymn of this kind usually shops. What the word insists on is parity. A counter-stake is by definition equal in value to what it answers, or the wager will not stand. Kāmeśvara's love is called a ratna and a maṇi, a jewel; she does not receive it, she matches it.

That is worth holding against the ordinary run of Sanskrit love poetry, where a woman's body is what a man pays for or dies for. Here it is what she pays with, and she is the party setting the terms. The name also follows directly on from the marriage cord of the previous verse, which makes the sequence look deliberate: a contract was tied at the throat, and this is the consideration.

The second name changes register completely and becomes technical in a different field. Ālavāla is not a poetic word. Monier-Williams gives it one sense and one only — a basin for water round the root of a tree — and it belongs beside parivāha in the sixth verse, the overflow channel of an irrigation tank. This hymn keeps reaching for the vocabulary of water management on land, and both times the effect is the same: the image stops being decorative and becomes something a person could actually dig.

Śaṅkara's verse on the navel makes the identical identification and then extends it into a list of five. Her navel is a whirlpool of the Ganges standing still; it is the basin at the root of the creeper of her line of down, with her breasts for its buds; it is the fire-pit for the flame that is the heat of the flower-arrowed god; it is Rati's pleasure-house; and it is the mouth of the cave in which Śiva's eyes reach their perfection. One word differs from the sahasranāma and the difference is the whole of the poetry. Śaṅkara says mukula, bud; this hymn says phala, fruit. Same plant, two moments in its year. A bud is a promise, and fruit is what a creeper is for.

The fire-pit in the middle of that list deserves a moment. Śaṅkara calls the navel a kuṇḍa, which is the word the fourth name of this stotra used when it said she came up out of a cidagnikuṇḍa, a fire-pit made of awareness. In his verse the fire in the pit is Kāma's heat; in the fourth name it is consciousness. The same vessel with a different fuel, and the whole narrative the hymn sits inside was set going by what happened when Kāma's fire and Śiva's fire were brought together.

Śaṅkara also gives the line of down an origin myth, and it is the darkest of his conceits about her body. Kāma, his body licked over by the ranks of flame that were Śiva's anger, plunged into the deep pool of her navel; and the thin line of smoke that rose out of it afterwards is what people take for her romāvali. That is the burning of the god of desire — the event that produces the ash out of which Bhaṇḍāsura is fashioned, which is why she rose from the fire in the fourth name of this hymn — relocated onto her body as a line of hair. The creeper in the garden and the smoke from a cremation are the same line, described by two poets who both knew the story.

One grammatical detail that changes how the verse sounds. Both names here end in long ī rather than the long ā that closes almost everything else in the hymn: stanī and kucadvayī. They are bahuvrīhi compounds whose final members, stana and dvaya, have been given the feminine ī when made to agree with her. Nothing doctrinal follows from it, but the ear notices, and it is the same shift that produced kacchapī three verses ago and will produce jaṅghikā two verses on.
commentary.practice:
Two sixteen-syllable names again, and both caesurae fall at a joint in the compound: kāmeśvarapremaratna, then maṇipratipaṇastanī; nābhyālavālaromāli, then latāphalakucadvayī.

The consort is named for the third time in four verses and this is the long form. Kāmeśa at names 28 and 30, kāmeśvara here, kāmeśa again at 39. It is the same god and the choice is metrical: kāma plus īśa, kāma plus īśvara, each compressing by the same merger of a and ī into e. Two invisible seams, and worth undoing once out loud — kāma-īśvara — so that the name does not become a single opaque block.

Prema is not a stem in its own right. The dictionary form is preman, a neuter noun in -an, and it drops its final n inside a compound exactly as paribhāvin and samākarṣin did in the ninth and tenth verses, and as dāman will in the very next verse. Collect these: the loss of a final n in compound is one of the three or four habits that account for most of the odd-looking word-shapes in this hymn.

Pratipaṇa contains the best single piece of phonetics in the verse. Its ṇ is retroflex, and it is retroflex because of the r in prati — the ṇatva rule the pilot pointed out at ābharaṇa in the seventh verse. Here the r and the ṇ are separated by two whole syllables and the rule still reaches across them. That reach is exactly what makes the rule remarkable, and hearing it work at this distance is more instructive than any statement of it. Say pra-ti-pa-ṇa with a genuine curl on the last consonant.

The second line opens on a kind of sandhi you have not met yet in this hymn. Nābhi plus ālavāla does not merge into a long vowel; the i of nābhi turns into the consonant y, giving nābhyālavāla, written नाभ्यालवाल with the bh carrying a y underneath. Sanskrit does this whenever i or u meets a dissimilar vowel: i becomes y, u becomes v. Undoing it is how you find nābhi in the dictionary, and it is a good deal harder to spot than the a plus a mergers you are used to by now.

Romāli hides two things at once. Roman, the hair of the body, has lost its final n, and the resulting romā has merged with the ā of āli, a row. So romāli is roman plus āli with two operations applied in sequence, and neither is visible.

After that the line lets go: latā, phala, kuca, dvayī are all short, open and easy, and the only care needed is on dvayī, where the dv is a dental d followed by a labiodental v and both must be heard. English speakers reduce it to one or the other.

There is almost no retroflex traffic in this verse — the ṇ of pratipaṇa and nothing else — which after several verses of heavy ṭ and ḍ and ṇ is itself worth noticing. The tongue stays forward. Let it.

For the archanā, the datives are kāmeśvarapremaratnamaṇipratipaṇastanyai namaḥ and nābhyālavālaromālilatāphalakucadvayyai namaḥ. Both are ī-stems, and the second gives you a doubled y in the ending, dvay-yai, which is unusual enough that reciters often smooth it away.

On what to hold: the two names give two incompatible accounts of one thing, and the hymn does not reconcile them. In the first, nothing is given away and nothing is received; a price is met exactly. In the second, nothing is bought at all; something was planted, watered and left alone, and in due course it bore. Chanting them in succession without deciding between them is the discipline this poem asks for over and over.

015.subtitle: A waist arrived at by argument

commentary.meaning: The most peculiar name in the whole head-to-foot description, and the only one that is an inference rather than an observation. Her waist cannot be seen. What can be seen is the line of down; a creeper has to be growing on something; therefore there is a waist. Samunneya is the word for what has to be deduced, and the name is put together like a step in an argument rather than a piece of description — the smoke is visible, so there is fire. Then the second name looks at the same place and finds it in trouble. The middle is splitting under the weight above it, and the three folds of skin across it are doing the work of a bandage tied round a break. Nothing anywhere else in this body has been in any danger. The description has reached the one part of her that is described as failing, and it spends two whole names saying so.
commentary.history:
The thin waist is the oldest and most worn of all the conventions of Sanskrit description, and by itself it would be worth no comment. What is not conventional is the vocabulary this name reaches for. Lakṣya is what is perceptible, what can be marked or observed; ādhāratā is an abstract noun meaning the condition of being a support; samunneya is what is to be inferred or deduced. Not one of these belongs to poetry. They belong to the vocabulary of Indian logic, where the standing example of a valid inference is the fire on the mountain deduced from the smoke above it. The Vāgdevatās have dropped a small piece of Nyāya into a love poem and produced a name that has to be reasoned through rather than looked at.

Śaṅkara asks the same question — what is it that is actually visible at her waist? — and gives an answer stranger than any inference. It is the sky. Space got in between her two jar-like breasts, was thinned to a thread by their pressing against one another, and is now going into the cavern of her navel; and that thread of squeezed sky, dark and shaped like the very finest ripple on the Yamunā, is what discerning eyes make out at her middle. Both poets agree that there is nothing there. One says: therefore reason to it. The other says: therefore what you are seeing is the sky.

The three folds have a name of their own in the language. Monier-Williams enters trivali as a word and glosses it, drily, as the three folds over a woman's navel, regarded as a beauty. It is standard descriptive furniture. What this name does with it is not standard, because it makes the folds functional: they are a paṭṭabandha, and the middle would give way without them.

Paṭṭa is the item to look up. The dictionary gives it as a slab or tablet; as the copper plate on which a royal grant is inscribed; as the flat surface of anything; as a bandage, ligature, strip or fillet of cloth; and then as a frontlet or turban, of which it specifies five kinds — those of kings, of queens, of princes, of generals, and the turban of honour. So one word covers a surgical dressing and a crown-cloth. Paṭṭabandha is accordingly both the tying on of a bandage and the tying on of a diadem, and the ceremony by which a king is installed is a paṭṭābhiṣeka — which is one of the events Agastya lists in the frame narrative of this stotra among the things he has already been taught, and which lies behind the third name of the hymn, mistress of the splendid lion-throne. The folds that are splinting her waist are wearing the same word as her coronation.

Śaṅkara makes the same observation without the pun and with a good deal more anxiety. Her waist, he says, is thin by nature, worn out by the weight of the slopes of her breasts, bowed under it, seeming to give way little by little; its steadiness is the steadiness of a tree left standing on a riverbank after the bank has gone. And then, in the last words of the verse, he does something a hymn of praise is not supposed to do: he wishes it well. May it long be safe. It is one of the few places in the poem where the speaker stops admiring and starts worrying.

His next verse supplies the agent that the sahasranāma leaves out. The breasts split the bodice moulded on them and chafe at the roots of her arms; the bodiless god, judging that this was quite enough to break her waist, has bound it in three places to save it, as one ties lengths of lavalī creeper round something. So the trivali is a splint, and the person who applied it is Kāma — which returns the whole image to the inventory of his equipment that the second and third verses of this hymn put in her hands.

One structural point, so that the sequence does not seem disordered. Verse fourteen named her breasts twice, this verse names them again in the first element of its second name, and the description has now circled the same region of the body for three names running. That is normal for the form; the middle of the body is where these poems always slow down most. The descent resumes in earnest at the next verse, when she is finally dressed.
commentary.practice:
Two sixteen-syllable names, and for the first time in several verses one of the caesurae is awkward. Count eight in the first line and you land inside a word: lakṣyaromalatādhā | ratāsamunneyamadhyamā. The pause falls between dhā and ra, in the middle of ādhāratā. Hear the break without opening a gap in the sound, exactly as the pilot advised for the fourth meditation verse. The second line behaves: stanabhāradalanmadhya, then paṭṭabandhavalitrayā, and the break is at a joint.

Lakṣya opens on kṣ, which you met at ikṣu in the third verse: an unvoiced velar k running straight into the retroflex sibilant ṣ, and never the English x. Then y. Lak-ṣya.

Ādhāratā is worth taking apart, because the suffix is what turns this name into an argument. Sanskrit makes abstract nouns freely with -tā and -tva, exactly as English makes them with -ness and -ity. Ādhāra is a support; ādhāratā is the state of being a support. So the compound says that her waist is to be inferred from the visible line of down's being supported by something. Remove the two syllables of -tā and you have a picture; leave them in and you have a premise.

Samunneya is sam plus ud plus the root nī with the gerundive ending -ya, and the d of ud has assimilated forward to give a doubled n. Written समुन्नेय. Both n must be heard, and the metre requires the first syllable to be heavy on the strength of them: sa-mun-ne-ya.

The second line gives you the seventh or eighth compound-final present participle of the hymn, and this one is disguised. Dalat, splitting, has run into madhya, and its final t has assimilated to the following m to become n: dalanmadhya. That is the same change you saw at calanmīna in the sixth verse. Once you know to look for it, an -an- in front of a nasal is very often a hidden -at.

Paṭṭa is the single hardest sound in the verse and the only retroflex in it. A doubled retroflex ṭ: the tongue-tip curls back, makes the closure, holds it, and releases into the second. There is no forward movement in between, and the doubling must be audible or the syllable will not be heavy. Everything else in the line — stana, bhāra, dalan, madhya, bandha, vali, traya — is dental or labial, so the tongue is forward throughout and curls back exactly once. Practising the line for that one contrast is a better use of two minutes than practising it for speed.

Bandha has an aspirated dh after a dental n; give the breath its own release. Valitrayā ends the line on three light syllables and a long one, which lets the verse land softly after a heavy middle.

One merger to reconstruct: latā plus ādhāratā gives latādhāratā, with two long ā swallowing each other into one and no trace of it in either script.

For the archanā, lakṣyaromalatādhāratāsamunneyamadhyamāyai namaḥ and stanabhāradalanmadhyapaṭṭabandhavalitrayāyai namaḥ. The second is one of the longest datives in the first hundred names and worth saying slowly once on its own.

On what to hold: this verse offers a contemplative instruction more precise than most. Take the first name exactly as it is constructed. You cannot see the thing itself. You can see what it holds up. Therefore it is there. That is the shape of every inference anyone has ever made about the subject of this hymn, and the Vāgdevatās have written it into a description of a waist.

016.subtitle: Safflower on the slope, and a belt that speaks first

commentary.meaning: The garment at last — the first clothing named anywhere in this hymn. It is dyed with safflower, and the colour is given twice over, aruṇa aruṇa, dawn-red and red, which is the Sanskrit way of saying very red indeed. Light is on it: bhāsvat, shining, one more of the present participles this poem runs on. And the surface the cloth lies along is called a taṭī, a slope, which is the word used of a mountainside and of a riverbank. Then the belt, and with it the verse changes sense entirely. Small bells set with gems hang on the cord around her waist, so that whenever she moves she is heard before she is seen. One name is nothing but colour and light; the other is nothing but sound; and in the order of experience the second comes first.
commentary.history:
Kusumbha is safflower, Carthamus tinctorius, and kausumbha is the adjective from it: dyed with safflower, orange-red. This was the everyday red of Indian dyeing, cheap beside madder or lac, and it gives a brilliant orange-scarlet that no other plant matches. It is also notoriously fugitive. Safflower red fades in light faster than almost any other natural dye, and Monier-Williams records the figurative sense that the fact produced: kusumbha also means outward affection, so called, he says, by comparison with the colour of safflower. The word for the dye became a word for love that washes out. There is no reason at all to think the Vāgdevatās meant a rebuke by it, and the plain sense of the name is simply that her cloth is red. But it is worth knowing that of every red available the poem has chosen the one that does not last, for a goddess whose signature colour is the sky in the few minutes before sunrise.

The doubling of aruṇa is intensive. Sanskrit repeats a word to strengthen it, and the second aruṇa is not a second colour but the same colour insisted on; the alternative reading, which the grammatical note on this name prefers, takes the pair as a comparison, dawn-red set against plain red. Either way the redundancy is deliberate, and by this point in the hymn the reader should be counting. Sindūra and aruṇa in the meditation verses; a thousand rising suns; a flood of red light drowning the world-eggs; the ruby diadem; the ruby mirror; coral and the bimba fruit; and now a red garment described as red twice. At name forty-nine the hymn will give up qualifying and simply call her sarvāruṇā, red throughout.

Kaṭītaṭī is a landscape word attached to a body. Kaṭi is the hip — Monier-Williams also gives, unexpectedly, the entrance of a temple and an elephant's cheek — and taṭī is the feminine of taṭa, a slope, a declivity, a bank. The usage is entirely standard; the same taṭa turns up as stanataṭa, the slope of the breast, in the Saundaryalaharī verse quoted in the previous module. What is not standard is how literally Śaṅkara takes it. In his verse on the same feature, the lord of mountains cuts weight and breadth out of his own slope and settles them on her as a wedding gift, so that the wide heavy sweep of her hips now covers the whole earth over and makes light of it. Her father gave her a piece of himself, and the piece was a hillside.

The word Śaṅkara uses there, nitamba, is itself worth a look, because Monier-Williams gives four senses in a row and they are all in play in this stretch of the hymn: the buttocks, especially of a woman; figuratively, the ridge or side or swell of a mountain and the sloping bank of a river; the shoulder; and — this is the surprise — the sounding-board of a vīṇā. Five verses after the kacchapī lute was shamed into silence, the description has arrived at the part of the body that shares its name with the lute's resonator.

The belt is the more interesting of the two names because it is about being heard. Raśanā is a rope, a rein, a bridle, and a woman's girdle; dāman is a cord; kiṅkiṇikā is a small bell, and the word is simply the noise one makes. So the ornament is a cord slung round the hips with jewelled bells strung on it. Sanskrit poetry cares about this ornament more than about any other, and the reason is acoustic: the girdle is how a woman's approach is known. The Saundaryalaharī's own portrait of this goddess opens on it — before a single feature of her body is named, the first two syllables of the verse are kvaṇat, sounding, and the first thing described is her girdle-cord.

Two pieces of vocabulary carry further than they look. Kāñcī, the commonest ordinary word for this girdle, is glossed by Monier-Williams as a woman's zone furnished with small bells and other ornaments — and then, in the same entry, as the name of one of the seven sacred cities, the Kāñcī of the far south which is among the great seats of this goddess's worship and which the hymn will reach in its own way at name sixty-two. And the hymn comes back to the bells themselves: at name three hundred and twelve she is raṇatkiṅkiṇimekhalā, girdled with ringing bells, the same bells and a different word for the belt, two hundred and seventy names later.

One last observation about where this verse sits. From the eleventh verse to the fifteenth the description has worked down through the mouth, chin, throat, arms, breasts, navel and waist, and everything named has been skin, jewel, flower or thread. This is the hinge at which she is dressed. From here the descent passes over the garment to the thighs, knees, shanks, ankles and feet, and the safflower cloth named here is the last thing the poem interposes between the reciter and her.
commentary.practice:
The first line is much the harder of the two and all of its difficulty is in the vowels. Aruṇa plus aruṇa gives aruṇāruṇa: the two words have merged at the seam into a single long ā that belongs to neither of them. Written अरुणारुण. Say a-ru-ṇā-ru-ṇa slowly enough to feel that the first ṇ and the second ṇ are the same consonant occurring in two different words, and that the long vowel in the middle is the join. Both ṇ are retroflex, and this is the drill the pilot set at sindūrāruṇa in the first meditation verse, now doubled and with nothing else in the line to hide behind.

Kausumbha shows a piece of derivation you have already met once. The vowel-strengthening called vṛddhi turns the u of kusumbha into au, exactly as it turned the u of sugandha into saugandhika in the fourth verse and turns sundara into saundarya in the title of Śaṅkara's poem. Then mbh: a labial nasal running into an aspirated labial, and the aspiration must be released rather than swallowed.

Vastra gives you str, three consonants with one vowel among them, all dental or near it. Bhāsvat is the hymn's eighth compound-final present participle in -at — after udyat, majjat, lasat, kanat, vibhrājat, calat and dalat — and here it runs straight into a k: bhāsvatkaṭītaṭī, an unvoiced dental t immediately followed by an unvoiced velar k. The t will vanish if you let it. Release it.

The line then ends on a small drumming figure that is one of the pleasures of the verse: ka-ṭī-ta-ṭī, two retroflex ṭ, two long ī, and a short a in between them. Curl the tongue back for both and let the two long vowels ring.

The second line is easier and mostly nasal. Kiṅkiṇikā puts a guttural ṅ before k and then a retroflex ṇ, so within four syllables the tongue makes a nasal at the velum and then a nasal with the tip curled right back: kiṅ-ki-ṇi-kā. It is a good, short exercise in the fact that Sanskrit has five distinct nasals and expects all of them.

Raśanā has the palatal ś; keep it distinct from the dental s of kausumbha and vastra in the line above. Dāman appears as dāma-, having lost its final n inside the compound, exactly as preman did in the previous verse — the second instance in two verses of the same habit, which makes this a good moment to fix it.

Both caesurae are well behaved and fall at joints: aruṇāruṇakausumbha, then vastrabhāsvatkaṭītaṭī; ratnakiṅkiṇikāramya, then raśanādāmabhūṣitā.

One word to enjoy rather than to drill: ramya, delightful. It is a gerundive from √ram, to take pleasure, so it means to-be-enjoyed, in the same way that kamanīya in the thirteenth verse meant to-be-desired. Monier-Williams also records ramya as a name for the campaka tree, which has been in this hymn twice already.

For the archanā, aruṇāruṇakausumbhavastrabhāsvatkaṭītaṭyai namaḥ and ratnakiṅkiṇikāramyaraśanādāmabhūṣitāyai namaḥ. Note that the ī-stem taṭī contracts to taṭyai while the ā-stem takes the full -āyai, which is the same contrast the eleventh verse offered.

On what to hold: the verse conveniently divides the attention between two senses, and the order it puts them in is the wrong way round on purpose. Read the line about colour first, as written. Then notice that in any actual encounter the bells would have been heard from the next room, before there was anything at all to look at.

017.subtitle: What only her husband knows, and two crowns of ruby

commentary.meaning: The description crosses below the garment and immediately runs into a problem, which it solves by declining to solve it. The thighs are named, and what is said about them is that their grace and their softness are known — and known to exactly one person. It is a piece of discretion built into the poem: the hymn goes on describing and at the same moment hands the description over to somebody else and steps back. Then the knees, and the reticence stops at once. There is nothing withheld about them: they are round and glowing and shaped like a pair of small crowns cut out of ruby. Two names about one leg, one of which withholds and one of which displays, and the ruby of the second brings the colour back the instant the discretion is over.
commentary.history:
The first name is put together oddly, and the oddity is the point. Jñāta is a past participle, known; saubhāgya and mārdava, grace and softness, are what is known; and Kāmeśa, in compound, is the one who knows them. The tradition reads the name two ways at once and does not choose. On the plain reading it is modesty: this is the part of the body a husband sees, and the hymn says so instead of describing it. On the other reading jñāta is doing technical work — what is known here is known by direct acquaintance rather than by report, and Kāmeśa is not a censor but the only qualified witness. Both senses are in the word and neither cancels the other.

Śaṅkara makes the same claim about exclusivity at a different point on the body and states it as a comparison between goddesses. How many and how many poets do not enjoy Brahmā's wife — Sarasvatī is taken by anyone who writes. Who fails to become the husband of Śrī, given a little money? But contact with this goddess is not to be had by anybody except Mahādeva, not even by the kuravaka tree; and the kuravaka is the tree that, by long convention, flowers when a beautiful woman embraces it, so it is the one thing in the poetic world that gets to touch every woman there is. Denying it access is the strongest form the claim can take.

Then the knees, and here the parallel is exact rather than thematic. Śaṅkara devotes one verse to thighs and knees together and gives both their comparisons. Her two thighs have defeated the trunks of lordly elephants and the golden stems of the plantain — the two stock similes for a smooth tapering limb, disposed of in half a line. And her two knees, well-rounded and hardened by bowing to her husband, are the pair of frontal globes on the elephant of the gods.

Praṇatikaṭhina, hardened by prostration, is the detail to stop on. The knees of a goddess whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva are all said to worship are calloused because she kneels. The first verse of the Saundaryalaharī says that without her Śiva cannot so much as stir; the eighty-second says her knees are hard from bowing to him. The tradition holds the two together without any sense of strain, and so does this hymn, which will seat her on Śiva's lap at name fifty-two and then, two names later, call her the woman whose beloved is entirely under her own control.

A textual note, since the manuscripts disagree here. The third line of that Saundaryalaharī verse is transmitted in two forms: the Śṛṅgeri text reads vidhijñe, a vocative meaning you who know the rite, while other printed editions read vijigye, you have conquered, which makes the knees the subject of a second verb. The picture is the same either way. It is worth knowing that this poem, like the sahasranāma, has been copied for a very long time and shows it.

The ruby is the fourth red stone in the hymn and the third distinct word for one. Māṇikya is the ordinary word and the first meditation verse used it for her crown; kuruvinda was the stone strung in her diadem at name fourteen; padmarāga was her cheek at name twenty-one. What is new here is the shape. The knee is not compared to a ruby but to a crown made of ruby, so an ornament that sat on top of her head at the beginning of the description turns up again at the knee in miniature. Monier-Williams defines mukuṭa as a tiara or diadem and adds that it is said to be crescent-shaped, distinguishing it from the pointed kirīṭa and the three-pointed mauli. A crescent is exactly the outline of a kneecap seen straight on.

What the two names do together is worth naming, because it is a structural problem solved rather than an image invented. The head-to-foot form obliges the poet to keep going. Between the waist and the ankle there is a stretch of the body that a hymn addressed to a mother cannot describe in the manner of erotic poetry and cannot skip either. This verse is the way out, and it is a good one: one name that says the information exists and is not being handed over, and one name that returns to plain visual description as soon as it decently can.
commentary.practice:
Two sixteen-syllable names, both with the caesura at a clean joint: kāmeśajñātasaubhāgya, then mārdavorudvayānvitā; māṇikyamukuṭākāra, then jānudvayavirājitā.

The conjunct ज्ञ in kāmeśajñāta is the same one the pilot drilled at mahārājñī in the first verse, and this is the shape in which you will meet it most often. It is a palatal j followed by the palatal nasal ñ, both made with the tongue-body flat against the hard palate. Reciters trained in the north approximate it as something like gy and reciters trained in the south as something like jñ; the grammarians describe the latter. You will need it constantly from here on — jñāna, prajñā, vijñāna, sarvajñā all take it.

Saubhāgya is a vṛddhi formation and so is mārdava, and having two of them side by side makes the process visible. Subhaga, fortunate, strengthens its u to au and becomes saubhāgya, good fortune. Mṛdu, soft, strengthens its syllabic ṛ to ār and becomes mārdava, softness. The last verse gave you kusumbha becoming kausumbha by the same rule; the fourth verse gave you sugandha becoming saugandhika. Collect them, because once vṛddhi is audible, half the abstract nouns in Sanskrit stop looking arbitrary.

Mārdava plus ūru gives mārdavoru: a short a and a long ū have merged into a single o, written मार्दवोरु with one ो and no trace of the join. This is the same merger that produced tapanoḍupa in the eighth verse and it has the same consequence — ūru will not be found in the dictionary in the shape it has here, and you have to undo the sandhi before you can look it up. Note also that ūru begins with a long ū, which English speakers shorten.

Dvaya occurs twice in the verse, at ūrudvaya and jānudvaya, and the dv is a dental d followed by a labiodental v with both audible. English tends to drop one or the other.

The second line is where the tongue goes back. Māṇikya has the retroflex ṇ, mukuṭa has the retroflex ṭ, and then the line comes forward again for jānu, dvaya and virājitā, all of which are dental or palatal. Curl back twice and return, and do not let the ṇ of māṇikya soften into the n of jānu three syllables later — they are the same drill the pilot set at sindūrāruṇa and trinayanāṃ.

Mukuṭa plus ākāra gives mukuṭākāra, one more of the invisible a-plus-ā mergers that this hymn is built out of.

The verse ends on virājitā, the same past participle that ended the first name of the twelfth verse — cibukaśrīvirājitā there, jānudvayavirājitā here. Five verses apart, the identical closing word, and it is a good marker to have in the ear: whenever a line ends -virājitā, something has been made resplendent by something else, and the something else is named just before it.

For the archanā, kāmeśajñātasaubhāgyamārdavorudvayānvitāyai namaḥ and māṇikyamukuṭākārajānudvayavirājitāyai namaḥ.

On what to hold: the verse gives a real instruction about the limits of looking, and it is the more effective for being unmarked. The first name tells you that there is something here you are not going to be told. It does not apologize for it, hint at it, or invite you to imagine it. Most descriptive poetry works by promising more than it delivers; this one works by declining, and then goes straight on to the knees, which is exactly what the reciter should do.

018.subtitle: Quivers strewn with rain-insects, and the arch of the foot

commentary.meaning: Three names, and the verse breaks the pattern of the last several by fitting a very short one between two long. The shanks first, tapering like the quivers of the god of love and scattered over with indragopa, the small brilliant scarlet insects that come up out of the ground with the first rain. Then, in four syllables, the ankles: hidden. No bone stands out, nothing shows through, which in the descriptive tradition is the mark of a body finished properly. Then the instep, which is said to beat the domed back of a tortoise at its own game — the smooth unbroken rising curve that the comparison was invented for, outdone by the thing it was invented to describe. The description has reached the feet, and it will stay there for the rest of this verse and the whole of the next.
commentary.history:
Indragopa is a real animal and a fixed poetic signal. Monier-Williams gives it as the cochineal insect of various kinds, and as a firefly; what is generally meant is the tiny bright red velvet mite that appears in enormous numbers on wet ground within a day or two of the first monsoon rain, all over India — a scrap of scarlet velvet about the size of a grain of rice. Sanskrit poets use it as the sign that the rains have begun, the way English poets use the cuckoo for spring. Its name means Indra's cowherd, or the one Indra protects, and Indra is the god who sends the rain.

What the name does with it is not what a poet usually does. The insects are not simply present on the ground; they are parikṣipta, scattered over or strewn about the quiver itself. So the picture is a leather case flecked all over with points of scarlet, and an entire monsoon convention has been converted into upholstery. Whether the flecks are meant to be the natural mottling of her skin or the insects themselves crawling on it, the poem does not say, and the ambiguity is probably the point.

The quiver is Kāma's, so this is the fifth or sixth time his equipment has been found on her: the noose and goad in the second verse, the sugarcane bow and five arrows in the third, the wedding arch and the fish-banner at her eyebrows and eyes in the sixth, and now his quivers for her shins. The word tūṇa is derived by Monier-Williams from √tul, so a quiver is literally a bearer. The comparison is entirely about shape — a quiver tapers from a wide mouth to a narrow foot, exactly as a calf tapers to an ankle.

Then jaṅghikā, which is a diminutive. Monier-Williams's headword is jaṅghā, the shank from ankle to knee, and jaṅghikā appears in the dictionary only as an equivalent of it, with a cross-reference and nothing more. The affectionate small form, dropped into the middle of a martial image, is one of the quieter pieces of tenderness in the hymn.

Śaṅkara takes the same figure and does arithmetic with it, and it is his best piece of counting. In order to defeat Rudra, he says, the god of the uneven arrows has certainly made her two shanks into a pair of quivers loaded with twice his usual number of shafts. How does one know? Because at the tips of them ten arrow-heads can be seen, disguised as the nails at the ends of her two feet, and whetted on the single whetstone which is the crowns of the gods. Kāma carries five arrows; two quivers of five make ten; and there are exactly ten toenails. The heads are sharp because so many gods have bowed at those feet that their diadems have polished them. The sahasranāma will pick up those toenails in the very next verse, and a reader who has this in mind will know why they shine.

Gūḍhagulphā is the shortest name the hymn has produced so far, and all it says is that a joint does not show. Concealed ankles belong to the old repertoire of the well-made body, in which any prominent bone anywhere is a defect and the ideal limb is one whose structure is not legible through the skin. The brevity is itself an effect: after sixteen syllables of quiver and insect the poem says two words and moves on.

The tortoise is the standard comparison for the top of a foot and the reason is exact rather than fanciful. A tortoise carapace rises in a single continuous dome with no ridge and no break in it, which is precisely what an instep does. The name says her instep is jayiṣṇu over it, victorious — the same figure the ninth verse used to dispose of coral and the bimba fruit.

Śaṅkara, characteristically, will not defeat the comparison; he quarrels with it. How, he asks, did good judges ever come to weigh your instep against the hard shell of a tortoise? And how did the breaker of the three cities, at the time of the wedding, take it up in both hands and set it down on the stone, with a heart full of pity? The second question is the one that matters. He is referring to the aśmārohaṇa, the mounting of the stone, a step in the classical wedding in which the groom places the bride's foot on a millstone and asks her to be as firm as it is. Śaṅkara is objecting that a foot which had to be handled that carefully cannot be the same foot the poets compare to something hard, and the answer he leaves unspoken is that it is soft and the comparison is a slander. The sahasranāma keeps the tortoise and simply lets her win.

One small resonance. The tortoise has been in this hymn before under a different word: the lute of the eleventh verse, kacchapī, is named for its tortoise-shaped body. Two tortoises seven verses apart, one shouted into silence and one overtaken. And two references to the wedding rite within nine names, the thread at the throat and the stone here, which is a reminder that this hymn assumes throughout that she is married. She is never once described as a maiden.
commentary.practice:
This is the first verse since the eighth to hold three names instead of two, and the arithmetic is sixteen, four, twelve. Indragopaparikṣiptasmaratūṇābhajaṅghikā fills the first line by itself; gūḍhagulphā takes four syllables of the second; kūrmapṛṣṭhajayiṣṇuprapadānvitā takes the remaining twelve. Getting that in the ear stops the verse from feeling lopsided.

Because a name ends inside the second line there is a genuine word-break after gulphā, and it should be audible. But the metre puts its caesura after the eighth syllable — gū-ḍha-gul-phā-kūr-ma-pṛ-ṣṭha — which falls inside the third name. So the sense break and the metrical break do not coincide, and you have to let one be heard without making the other. Articulate lightly after gulphā and let the metrical pause pass through the middle of kūrmapṛṣṭha without a gap, as at ādhāratā three verses ago.

The consonants here are the hardest in this whole range and the verse deserves to be drilled slowly. Parikṣipta puts kṣ and then pt into five syllables: pa-ri-kṣip-ta. Jaṅghikā has ṅgh, a guttural nasal running into a voiced aspirated velar, and the breath must be released. Gūḍha contains ḍh, the voiced retroflex aspirate that the pilot flagged at pāśāḍhyā in the second verse as one of the rarest and hardest sounds in the language: tongue-tip curled right back, voice on, and a distinct puff as it comes away. Gulpha has lph, an l into an aspirated p.

Pṛṣṭha is probably the single most difficult word in the first fifty names. It stacks the syllabic ṛ, the retroflex sibilant ṣ and the retroflex aspirated stop ṭh into one syllable: pṛṣ-ṭha, with the tongue-tip going back for the ṛ and staying back through the ṣ and the ṭh without coming forward at any point. Practise it alone before putting it back in the line.

The retroflex inventory for the verse is the largest so far: the ṣ of parikṣipta, the ḍh of gūḍha, the ṣ and the ṭh of pṛṣṭha, and the ṣ and the ṇ of jayiṣṇu. Six retroflexes in thirty-two syllables. Everything else — indra, gopa, smara, tūṇa apart from its ṇ, gulpha, prapada, anvitā — is dental or labial. The verse is therefore an unusually good exercise in the single contrast the whole phonology turns on.

Jayiṣṇu shows the ṇatva rule at short range: the retroflex ṣ pulls the following n back into the retroflex position and makes it ṇ. Two verses ago pratipaṇa showed the same rule triggered by an r across two syllables. Different trigger, same result, and between them they account for most of the retroflex nasals in this hymn.

One caution about the third name. Monier-Williams gives prapada as the point of the foot and the tips of the toes, and records the adverb prapadais, on tiptoe. The rendering used on this site, the fore part of the foot including the instep, is what the comparison with a tortoise's back requires, and it is what the commentators take; but the dictionary is narrower than the translation and it is worth knowing that.

Gūḍhagulphā is short enough to be memorized at once, and it is worth having by heart as a checkpoint: if you arrive at the second line and cannot find it, you have lost your place.

For the archanā, indragopaparikṣiptasmaratūṇābhajaṅghikāyai namaḥ, gūḍhagulphāyai namaḥ, kūrmapṛṣṭhajayiṣṇuprapadānvitāyai namaḥ. The middle one takes about a second and is a small relief in the middle of the sequence.

On what to hold: this verse is a fair test of whether the head-to-foot form can be taken on its own terms. There is no doctrine in an ankle. What the form asks is that the same quality of attention be spent on a joint that does not show as was spent on the flood of light in the third verse, and the tradition is entirely serious that this is a practice and not a distraction from one.

019.subtitle: Light off the toenails, and the lotus sent away

commentary.meaning: Two names about light coming off her feet, and the first of them is the first name since the fourth of the hymn to say what she does to a human being. The nails of her toes throw off a brightness; that brightness falls on the people bowing in front of them; and under it the tamas in those people is covered over and no longer shows. The verb matters: not burnt out, not destroyed, covered. Then the second name goes back to the contest form. Her two feet throw off so dense a mesh of light that the lotus — the standard against which every beautiful foot in Sanskrit has ever been measured — is not defeated but simply set aside, driven off the field. Between them the two names do the two things this hymn does over and over: they dispose of a convention, and they say quietly what the disposing is for.
commentary.history:
Dīdhiti is brightness, splendour, a ray; Monier-Williams also gives it, further down the entry, as religious reflection, devotion, inspiration. Toenails are a serious subject in this literature and not only because they catch the light. In the standard order of temple worship the devotee's head goes to the level of the deity's feet, so the toenails are literally the part of the image at eye height for somebody lying on the floor. When Śaṅkara says that the nails on her toes are moons bright enough to close the lotus-hands of the women of heaven, he is describing what is directly in front of the face of a person who has just prostrated.

Namajjana is namat, bowing, plus jana, people: the bowing folk. And what is covered in them is their tamoguṇa. The three guṇas of Sāṃkhya were already in play in the third verse of this hymn, where the five arrows turned out to be the tanmātras; sattva, rajas and tamas are the three strands of which everything material is woven, and tamas is the one that darkens and weighs down — inertia, obstruction, dullness of mind. Śrīvidyā has an interest in tamas that is not purely hostile, since the same word covers the darkness in which things rest, but the plain sense here is the ordinary one.

What the name claims is precise and unusually modest. Sañchanna means wholly covered, concealed. It does not say that the tamas is annihilated. It says that where her nail-light falls, the dullness is not visible. A stronger claim was available and the Vāgdevatās declined it, and the tradition reads the choice the way it reads several such names: what happens to a devotee first is not a change in what he is made of but a change in what is showing.

Śaṅkara gives her two feet a run of six verses in a row, from the eighty-fourth to the eighty-ninth, and one of them turns on exactly this point. Her feet, he says, seem to be laughing at the trees of heaven — laughing with their toenails, which are moons that make the lotus-hands of the celestial women close up. And what is the joke? The wish-granting trees hand out fruit with their sprout-fingertips, and only to those who are already in heaven; her feet give good fortune to the destitute, without pause and on the spot. The contrast is between a clientele that is already provided for and one that is not. It is the best short statement anywhere in this literature of what the tradition thinks a goddess's feet are for.

The lotus of the second name is the most exhausted comparison in the language. Padmapāda, caraṇakamala, pādāmbuja: the foot-lotus is so entrenched that it has stopped being a figure at all, and this hymn will itself use it in the very next verse, śrīpadāmbujā, having just thrown it out here. Saroruha, the word used here, means only risen out of a pool. Parākṛta means set aside, rejected, driven off, and it is a good deal more dismissive than defeated.

Śaṅkara argues the case rather than asserting it, and the three points he makes are the only place in either poem where a stock comparison is refuted with evidence. A lotus is a thing snow can kill; her feet are expert precisely at living on the snow mountain. A lotus shuts and sleeps at night; her feet are bright in the last watch of the night. A lotus is at best a vessel for Lakṣmī to stand in; her feet pour prosperity over the people who keep the observance. And then the shrug: what is remarkable, mother, in your two feet defeating a lotus? Three properties, three failures, and no more said.

One word in the second name deserves its own note. Jāla, in Monier-Williams, is first a net for catching birds or fish; then a hairnet; then a net in the figurative sense, a snare; and only by extension any dense collection or web. Prabhājāla is a mesh of light and the modern rendering is right, but the first sense of the word is a thing you catch something in. A hymn that opened its description of her hands with a noose has arrived at her feet and found another one.

Finally, a connection worth carrying. The toenails whose brightness this verse describes are the same ten nails that Śaṅkara, four verses earlier in his own poem, identified as the ten arrow-heads at the tips of the quivers that are her shanks, sharpened on the whetstone of the gods' crowns. If you take his account, the light coming off her nails is the shine of a weapon that has been polished by being bowed to.
commentary.practice:
Two sixteen-syllable names, and both caesurae fall at a joint: nakhadīdhitisañchanna, then namajjanatamoguṇā; padadvayaprabhājāla, then parākṛtasaroruhā.

Dīdhiti is easy to flatten and the metre will not allow it. Two long ī and then a short i: dī-dhi-ti, with an aspirated dh in the middle. Say it three times on its own before putting it into the line.

Sañchanna is a small demonstration of how Sanskrit spells assimilation, and it is worth more than the two seconds it takes. The prefix is sam. Before the palatal ch it becomes the palatal nasal ñ, so sam plus channa is written सञ्छन्न. The same prefix appears elsewhere in this stretch of the hymn as saṃ-, sam-, san- and saṅ-, and the five shapes are simply the five nasals, each chosen to match whatever follows. Once you see that, a whole class of apparently irregular spellings becomes predictable. Then give the doubled n of -channa its full length, because the metre counts on it.

Namajjana has the doubled palatal j, which is now the fifth appearance of that cluster in nineteen verses — ujjvalā twice, majjat twice, and here. Na-maj-ja-na.

Tamoguṇā hides one of the most productive sandhis in the language. Tamas plus guṇa gives tamoguṇa, because a final -as before a voiced sound becomes -o. Manas plus rūpa gave manorūpa in the third verse by exactly the same rule, and it accounts for an enormous number of the -o- compounds you will meet. Undo it and the s-stem underneath becomes findable. The ṇ of guṇa is retroflex and belongs to the stem; nothing triggers it.

The second line is the smoothest sixteen syllables in this whole range: pa-da-dva-ya-pra-bhā-jā-la-pa-rā-kṛ-ta-sa-ro-ru-hā. Only the dv of padadvaya and the syllabic ṛ of parākṛta ask for anything at all, and the rest is open. Use the line to check vowel length rather than agility, since there are five long vowels in it and eleven short, and the alternation is audible if you are doing it right.

One feature of the verse is worth noticing precisely because nothing calls attention to it: there is no palatal ś and no retroflex ṣ anywhere in it. Every sibilant here is the plain dental s, in sañchanna and saroruha. After the six retroflexes of the previous verse this is a clean stretch of road, and hearing the difference between one verse and the next is a better ear-training exercise than any drill.

For the archanā, nakhadīdhitisañchannanamajjanatamoguṇāyai namaḥ and padadvayaprabhājālaparākṛtasaroruhāyai namaḥ.

On what to hold: the first name is the place in the head-to-foot description at which the reciter is put into the picture. Everything from the hair down has been about her. This one is about the people bowing at her feet, and the person saying it is one of them. The instruction is not complicated and does not need to be dressed up: notice that the light is described as falling on you, and that what it does is cover something over rather than take it away.

crossReferences.translation: Caṇḍī, your two feet seem to be laughing at the trees of heaven — laughing with their toenails, which are moons that make the lotus-hands of the women of heaven close up. Those trees give fruit with their sprout-fingertips, and only to those already in heaven; your feet give good fortune to the poor, without pause and at once.
crossReferences.relevance: The same toenails and the same light, with the point of it spelled out. The wish-granting trees serve people who are already provided for; her feet serve people who are not. Read beside a name which says that her nail-light covers over the dullness of those who bow, it tells you who the bowing folk are taken to be.

crossReferences.translation: The lotus can be killed by snow; your feet are expert at nothing so much as living on the snow mountain. The lotus sleeps at night; your feet are bright in the last watch of the night. The lotus is at best a vessel for Lakṣmī to stand in; your feet pour out prosperity on those who keep the observance. Mother, what is remarkable in your two feet defeating a lotus?
crossReferences.relevance: The identical claim as the second name — the lotus loses — but argued instead of asserted, in three points, with the same word for lotus that the sahasranāma uses. It is the only place in either poem where a stock comparison is refuted with evidence rather than simply overthrown, and it explains why the hymn can dismiss the lotus here and then call her feet lotuses again in the very next verse.
